newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin wants compromise in Caucasus ethnic row.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin wants compromise in Caucasus ethnic row.

text.p: A Kremlin security official urged leaders of two North Caucasus regions on Monday to settle a border dispute that has raised fears of ethnic fighting, Russian news agencies said.

Concerns that an ancient conflict would revive were fuelled last week when 17 people were injured in an attack on a bus carrying Moslem Ingush refugees in Christian North Ossetia -- the worst of a number of such attacks this month.

"An escalation of violence in the region must be avoided at all costs," Mikhail Mityukov, deputy secretary of President Boris Yeltsin's Security Council, was quoted as telling a meeting of leaders from Ingushetia and North Ossetia.
Russia's volatile south has seen a host of ethnic squabbles as well as a full-scale war in Chechnya since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The refugees were among tens of thousands forced to flee their homes in North Ossetia's Prigorodny district five years ago, and were returning to the still-disputed area.

Nearly 200 people were killed in 1992 in the first major ethnic clashes within post-Soviet Russia in fighting over the district. The district, which lies close to the Ossetian capital of Vladikavkaz, used to belong to Ingushetia.

Ingush president Ruslan Aushev has accused North Ossetian leaders of sabotaging a repatriation programme to provoke a new conflict, and urged Yeltsin to impose direct Kremlin rule to avoid new bloodshed. He warned North Ossetia he was ready to protect the refugees.
North Ossetian leader Akhsarbek Galazov has rejected the charges and accuses Aushev of overreacting.
Mityukov told Ekho Moskvy radio after the meeting of the Security Council that the powerful advisory body opposed the idea of direct presidential rule because this "could only deepen the conflict".
He said experts would sum up proposals for Yeltsin, who is on holiday, on how to deal with the situation.

Hostility goes back centuries between the Ossetians, whose kin across the Caucasus mountains in South Ossetia won de facto autonomy in a war against Georgian troops in 1992, and the Ingush, whose Chechen kin defeated the Russian army last year.

Soviet dictator Josef Stalin deported the Ingush en masse to the Kazakh steppes in 1944, along with the Chechens, for allegedly collaborating with the invading German army. Some Ingush territory, including Prigorodny, was given to the Ossetians.
The Ingush were allowed to return to their lands in the late 1950s after Stalin's death but Prigorodny is still controlled by Ossetia.
